output:
Liora. The girl has questions. Questions that cut close to the bone. Perrin told her about the 400 sim set aside for the Holloways, and she wants to know why I don't just talk to them.

I look at her. Liora Thorne. My niece. She doesn't know what she doesn't know, and that's not her fault. But an answer suggests the telling is mine to give, and it is not.

What I cannot do is explain without breaking a forty-year promise to Nell Holloway. What I can do is what I've always done: cut more wood, eat less, let the thing settle itself.

Wren draws circles in her mind all night. I've heard her pacing. She thinks the debt is shameful, thinks her uncle knows something he won't say. She's right about the second part. But I won't be the one to end this, because I said I wouldn't, and that word still binds me even if we built the reason for it on sand.

I need to get to the forest. The morning's early, and work doesn't ask questions. Let them talk. Let them wonder. The trees don't need stories, only the axe.

"Aye," I say, because sometimes one word is enough, and sometimes it's all you've got. Then I go. I'm at the forest now. The air is clean, the work is honest, and nobody here asks about markers or forty-year-old promises. The trees stand where they stand. I fell them where they fall. That's the whole of it, and that's enough.

Corwin asks about the line. The west line, lightning oaks. He's serious about the work, my nephew, and that's why I brought him out here. He wants to know which trees, and I could mark them for him, or I could just tell him.

"The oaks," I say. "I marked three. Take the leaning one first—she'll fall clean onto the path."

That's the work. That's what we're here for. The rest of it, the thing with Wren and the marker and the forty years, none of that touches the ironwood grove. Out here a tree tells you what it will do before you swing, and you read it or you pay for misreading. Corwin knows enough to know he doesn't know enough yet. That's the beginning of knowing.

I should get to felling. The morning's young and wood doesn't stack itself. There's household mouths and the debt sitting heavy on Wren's mind. Four hundred sim doesn't earn itself, and neither do the answers nobody's paying me to give. </think>  The conversation is closed now, and Corwin goes to his work. I go to mine. The axe finds its rhythm, and the world narrows to the grain and the swing and the fall. This is the gift of it: when you're cutting true, there's no room for else.
